title: Vague Language Is a Cover for Bad Ideas
author: Mutually Assured Instruction
summary: Using Anna Stokke's line from researchED Melbourne — 'vague language is a cover for bad ideas' — as its organizing principle, this essay argues that Australian school leaders routinely adopt and promote programs whose evidence base collapses under even light scrutiny, precisely because vague language lets everyone avoid confronting how thin that evidence actually is. The author works through several concrete examples: a widely used resilience and emotional-literacy program whose sweeping confidence-and-relationship claims trace back to a study of just six schools and 46 students with no disclosed ages, and a statewide push for more physical activity in lessons that generalizes from a single Deakin University trial involving only Grade 1 and 2 students to every primary and secondary classroom. The piece also names the specific methodological weaknesses that let vague claims survive — pre/post survey designs vulnerable to a 'survey effect' where increased awareness of the questions inflates apparent gains, and studies whose own authors admit 'it is not possible to draw definitive conclusions' due to heterogeneity, a caveat the marketing built on top of the study omits. Citing Pamela Snow's warning that 'the middle of the road is where we are most likely to be hit by traffic from both directions' and Greg Ashman's observation that 'students tend to make poor choices about their learning,' the essay ultimately argues that vagueness in school leadership isn't usually malicious — it's often fear of taking a side in a contested debate — but that this fear-driven imprecision lets weakly evidenced programs spread unchecked through schools.
points: The case study of a resilience program whose sweeping claims rest on just six schools and 46 students with no disclosed year levels shows concretely how vague, confident program marketing can outrun a genuinely thin evidence base without anyone in the chain necessarily acting in bad faith.

Naming the specific 'survey effect' mechanism — where taking a pre-survey increases participants' awareness of what's being measured, inflating apparent post-survey gains — gives readers a portable methodological red flag to watch for in any program relying on before/after self-report surveys.

The essay's diagnosis that vague language often stems from leaders' 'fear of taking a stance in any debate' rather than malice reframes the problem as an organizational courage issue, directly linking Anna Stokke's and Pamela Snow's quotes about the cost of taking a clear position to the persistence of unscrutinized programs.
quotes: However, on closer inspection that idea is actually three toddlers in a trench coat trying to get into an R rated movie.

'Speaking your mind and taking a stand does come at a cost and can be wearing at times, but the middle of the road is where we are most likely to be hit by traffic from both directions.' - Pamela Snow

When digging deeper into the study conducted to make these conclusions it can be found that there were only six schools involved, a focus group of only 46 students, and no disclosure of the ages or year levels of the students taking part.

Using pre and post study surveys to justify results can be problematic because of the limitations of a 'survey effect' occurring where individuals in the initial survey lack the background knowledge to answer accurately

In the research cited to make these claims it then says 'it is not possible to draw definitive conclusions due to the level of heterogeneity in intervention components and academic-related outcomes assessed.'
Greg Ashman stated: 'Unfortunately, students tend to make poor choices about their learning' based on (Clark, 1982. Singer and Alexander, 2017. Foster, Rawson and Donlosky, 2018).
